style_spec.name: Classic 2D Documentary
style_spec.palette: Flat, readable hues — avoid neon/oversaturated color. Favor 2-4 dominant hues plus neutrals per scene so the image reads instantly, even at thumbnail size.
style_spec.shading: Restrained flat cel-shading, 1-2 tonal steps per surface (base, occasional shadow) — no painterly gradients, no hard outline on the shadow shapes themselves.
style_spec.summary: Bold 2D illustrated documentary style — thick confident outlines, rounded cartoon forms, and a restrained flat-shaded palette. Not hyper-realistic, not childish preschool cartoon, not generic corporate flat vector art.
style_spec.texture: A light, uniform paper/canvas grain overlay across the whole image — subtle enough to never read as noise or damage, present enough to avoid a flat vector-art look.
style_spec.lighting: Directional, motivated lighting with a clear implied light source and soft shadow shapes — never flat/shadowless, never harsh studio-flash lighting.
style_spec.linework: Thick, confident black outlines on every silhouette edge, with lighter interior detail lines. No sketchy cross-hatching, no photorealistic edge rendering.
style_spec.mapGrammar: Maps use a hand-illustrated cartographic style, not literally aged/parchment unless the topic calls for it. Place names and route lines are added programmatically — never baked into the image.
style_spec.perspective: Consistent one-to-two-point perspective per scene, eye-level or slightly low-angle by default for a grounded, cinematic feel.
style_spec.diagramGrammar: Diagrams use the same bold linework/palette as narrative scenes, never a generic flat corporate-infographic look. Labels and callouts are added programmatically in the video layer — never baked into the image.
style_spec.bodyProportions: Rounded, slightly simplified cartoon proportions with strong, instantly-readable silhouettes — not chibi, not hyper-stylized anime.
style_spec.faceConstruction: Expressive but simple faces — economical linework for eyes/brows/mouth, clearly readable expression. Avoid hyper-detailed photographic facial rendering and avoid oversized preschool-cartoon eyes.
style_spec.environmentDetail: Moderately detailed, readable environments and props with clear foreground/midground/background separation. Purposeful, uncluttered set-dressing — every visible object should feel intentional.
negativeConstraints: not generic corporate flat vector art

narrationSegments.text: A soft chime wakes the bunk and a band of blue‑white light rises along the wall. Through the porthole the horizon is the same thin red, but the tablet on the wall is decisive: three status icons—oxygen, water, power—line the top and read green, amber, green. A tap pulls open the morning checklist: ‘Life support check, forecast review, EVA readiness.’ That tap starts a chain: the crew verifies the life‑support indicators, scans the short exception log, and reads the day’s forecasts—those first checks convert Mars time into human priorities for the sol ahead.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: hook / scene setter

narrationSegments.text: A sol is almost an Earth day but runs about forty minutes longer. Operations handle that drift in two ways: during intense, short campaigns crews may 'live on Mars time'—shifting sleep and duty cycles gradually—otherwise planners lock activities to the sol and schedule around the daily slip so sleep and tasks stay reliable. On Base Alpha the lighting and the daily routines follow the sol: lights come up bright and blue at the start of the crew day and then slowly shift to warmer tones before sleep, which helps the body stay entrained to a 24.6597‑hour rhythm rather than slowly drifting out of phase.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: explain circadian context

narrationSegments.text: That tablet checklist is where automation and human judgment meet. Sensors and monitors continuously update the green/amber/red icons, but the crew still verifies them—reading the brief exception note, opening a recent sensor trace if something looks off, and deciding whether a local intervention is warranted. Dust and radiation forecasts appear next to the icons because those predictions gate what the crew can do: an amber dust forecast may defer an EVA or reschedule greenhouse lighting. In short: wake, check, decide—those three actions determine what gets done this sol and what must wait.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: establish morning gating logic and stakes

narrationSegments.text: A sol’s life‑support work reads like a choreography of small mechanical cues: a valve clicks, a blower ramps, a scrubber cycles through sorbent beds. Automated diagnostics run continuous health checks and reroute control loops to compensate for drift, but each morning a crew member walks the modules and performs hands‑on checks—reading filter pressure trends, feeling ducts for unexpected heat or vibration, and spot‑checking humidity at reference points. If an abnormal pressure rise appears they isolate the affected element, prepare the cartridge for replacement, and schedule a swap—one finding can cascade, pushing that maintenance ahead of planned EVAs or lab work and generating a spare‑part request before the sol’s timeline is finalized.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: describe life‑support chore reality

narrationSegments.text: Automation catches many routine deviations, but crews still run scheduled diagnostics and deal with surprises. A typical workflow looks like this: the automated log posts an exception; a technician pulls the relevant sensor trace, runs a handheld analyzer, then cross‑checks the onboard spare‑parts inventory. If a part is needed they assign the job to the maintenance officer, who records a priority and a target window for repair. On Base Alpha the morning inspection therefore typically includes a quick hands‑on glance at accessible scrubbers and filter housings—visual confirmation complements the automated green/amber markers—and any unresolved anomaly is handed off in the shift log so it won’t be forgotten overnight.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: explain maintenance workflows and handoffs

narrationSegments.text: In the greenhouse a faint hiss marks air movement through a growth rack and young lettuce unfurls beneath LEDs. Sensors track CO2, humidity, nutrient conductivity/pH and light intensity; control software nudges ventilation or nutrient dosing for small deviations, but people still perform the hands‑on tasks—seeding trays, pruning crowded plants, harvesting leaves and visually scanning for mold. When the morning checklist flags a greenhouse exception, it routes that alert to the agricultural specialist—because fresh greens are both morale and physiology, those human inspections and manual fixes keep the plant system functioning as part lab, part kitchen and part life‑support buffer.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: introduce greenhouse tempo and stakes

narrationSegments.text: Not all plant hardware is equal. Small, low‑power racks—think Veggie‑style setups—deliver modest, high‑value salad leaves and require frequent hands‑on care. Large, multi‑layer CEA modules can yield a lot per square meter but demand big, steady power and more automation. On Base Alpha the schedule balances both: the little racks usually operate continuously to supply part of the daily fresh food, while the power‑hungry vertical systems are brought online only when power forecasts and ISRU margins allow. That tradeoff shapes crew time: small racks cost more hands‑on labor per gram; large racks cost more energy but less per‑unit labor.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: explain tradeoffs between production modes

narrationSegments.text: Outside, surface tasks wait. Before any EVA the operations officer calculates an allowed dose for the suit based on the current environment and the mission's exposure policy, then converts that into a maximum allowed time for the planned walk. Planners batch surface tasks to make the most of each outing—one long paired EVA is often better than several short trips—because every airlock cycle costs time and every minute outside consumes radiation budget. Agencies and missions translate risk targets differently, so those allowed‑time calculations are done conservatively and tuned to the crew’s individual dosimetry.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: explain radiation budgeting and EVA chore choreography

narrationSegments.text: Dose rates on Mars vary with solar conditions and location; a reasonable open‑surface baseline is roughly a few hundred microsieverts per sol, with hourly rates on the order of a few hundredths of a millisievert. These are representative figures—the actual values depend on site and solar cycle—and solar particle events can spike exposures dramatically. That variability is why EVA planning always folds in SEP forecasts and why shelters and storm procedures are a hard requirement for surface operations.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: provide numbers and explain SEP risk

narrationSegments.text: Mid‑morning the uplink brings an updated dust forecast: regional dust mobilization could cut solar insolation over the next few sols. The power officer replays the day’s timeline against the new prediction—solar arrays will produce less, so batteries need more conservative cycling and any high‑power processes planned for peak sun are re‑examined. ISRU plants like MOXIE have startup and operating constraints, so the officer weighs whether to defer a planned production run or move it to a controlled, lower‑power standby; that decision changes what other loads—greenhouse lighting, charging schedules—are allowed to run today.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: introduce dust forecast as a scheduling stressor

narrationSegments.text: Priorities on Base Alpha are explicit: human life and habitat systems come first, followed by communications and essential science, then greenhouse support and ISRU, and last the discretionary work. When a dust forecast lowers expected solar the team trims from the bottom up—construction and elective cleaning pause, greenhouse supplemental lighting is dimmed, and ISRU is shifted from full production toward options that won’t risk depleting batteries. The power controller enforces the hierarchy in real time, so the colony can protect life‑critical loads while accepting delayed plant growth or postponed experiments.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: explain prioritization under reduced power

narrationSegments.text: A chamber alarm flags rising CO2. First, automated control loops reply—ventilation increases, scrubbers pulse, and the UI posts the corrective action taken. If those automatic steps can’t restore the setpoint, the agricultural specialist suits up for a targeted inspection: they check nutrient reservoirs and pumps, verify seals on air plenums, swab samples for contamination, and look for an unexpected respiration surge from a dense crop block. If contamination is suspected the protocol is immediate: isolate the chamber, bag samples for analysis, and transition trays to quarantine while the control loop and human inspection guide remediation.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: open greenhouse CO2 issue and show automation + manual handoff

narrationSegments.text: Meanwhile the EVA team is prepping a rover‑mounted drill sortie to collect outcrops for a geology campaign. One suit in the locker shows a fault code during pre‑flight diagnostics: a pressure‑regulation valve is reporting marginal response. The morning checklist's routing logic flags that suit and moves the planned EVA down the list until a technician can test and, if necessary, swap components. The suit fault cannot be ignored because a degraded regulator changes both the immediate safety envelope and the EVA's dose calculations.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: introduce suit maintenance open loop and safety response

narrationSegments.text: A quick diagnostic means technicians run a bench test, swap a filter if needed and perform a pressure hold. Because the operations chain integrated the morning check with technician schedules, the suit is returned to service within that sol's schedule and the mission can safely reassign the EVA team to a shortened field sortie later in the day. In other words: morning checks catch the problem, routing sends it to the right person, and the EVA is preserved without taking unnecessary risk.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: payoff: suit issue caught and routed to technician

narrationSegments.text: By mid‑afternoon the forecast proves prescient: dust thickens and solar output drops, so the battery state‑of‑charge starts toward a lower margin. The power officer flips the dust contingency: keep life‑support and medical loads powered, reduce greenhouse supplemental lighting and defer some growth cycles, and place the ISRU plant into a verified low‑power standby rather than an active production mode. To bridge the gap the team staggers ISRU tasks and leans on battery reserves; the consequence is straightforward—short‑term food growth slows and some science runs are deferred, but crew safety and breathable air remain protected.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: payoff: dust forecast forces battery/ISRU prioritization

narrationSegments.text: When the dust event tightened the power budget earlier, automated ventilation and scrubbers prevented CO2 from rising in most chambers. In the one flagged by the alarm the agricultural specialist performed a quick manual fix—checked and reseated a seal, verified ventilation dampers, and gave a small nutrient top‑off—and then confirmed the control loop accepted those inputs. The chamber’s CO2 returned to nominal over the following hours; because automation handled routine corrections and humans handled the seal and nutrient tasks, the problem didn’t cascade into longer, power‑intensive interventions.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: payoff: greenhouse CO2 resolved by automation + manual work

narrationSegments.text: The shortened EVA goes ahead during a lower‑dose window and the team keeps strict watch on individual dosimetry. They batch sampling tasks, stay close to the rover, and accept a shorter outing to keep cumulative mission exposure within the allocated budget. The day’s dose accounting is updated and the mission planners reassign lower‑priority outdoor tasks to later sols when radiation forecasts are more favorable.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: show how EVA scheduling adapts to dose constraints

narrationSegments.text: Late afternoon is when bodies and routines get serviced. Each crew member follows a scheduled mix of resistance exercises—elastic bands, a harnessed weight rig that loads legs in low gravity—and aerobic work on a treadmill or cycle to blunt muscle and bone loss. These sessions are slotted into the timetable like any other task because the habitat lighting system is tuned to reinforce them: bright, blue‑enriched spectra for active periods and gradual warming toward evening. Social activities—shared meals, a short group check‑in—are treated as operational requirements because predictable social time stabilizes morale and day‑to‑day performance, which in turn reduces human error during maintenance and critical decision windows.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: explain exercise and social scheduling as operational necessities

narrationSegments.text: When an alarm sounds the crew cannot expect an instant answer from Earth, so the routine is built to act locally. An instrument alarm first triggers onboard diagnostics and automated mitigation; if the problem persists a locally qualified specialist—often the person on the morning checklist—takes immediate steps: isolate the circuit, run handheld tests, and, if safe, enact a short repair. Only for problems that need expert analysis or policy changes is a message drafted to Earth and sent asynchronously. That practice reshapes who gets trained and the handoff discipline at shift changes: the person who fixes or defers a fault also documents the decision and signs the log so responsibility and context travel with the ticket, not with the delayed uplink.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: explain autonomy and decision‑making constraints

narrationSegments.text: As the sun sets across the basin the crew runs a formal end‑of‑sol routine. They export and archive life‑support logs, tag any alarms as cleared or deferred, and queue spare‑part orders for the next sol. Non‑critical tasks—construction checks, elective maintenance—are slipped into the next plan and annotated with expected power and crew needs. If an ISRU plant was running during the day, operators either schedule a controlled shutdown or set it to a low‑power standby so it won’t draw unpredictable loads overnight; that queued action appears in tomorrow’s timeline. The point is practical: catching and recording exceptions at closeout prevents small faults from vanishing between shifts and lets people sleep without an unresolved technical mystery nagging them.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: describe night checks and handoff practice

narrationSegments.text: The day closes with a human verification ritual. First the engineering lead reads aloud the status checklist—air scrubbers nominal, humidity within band, batteries holding a conservative reserve—and the maintenance officer confirms the suit repair log entry and the spare‑part ticket status. The ISRU array is left in a documented low‑power standby and greenhouse controllers show setpoints restored. Only then does the crew assemble in the common module: they light safe, synthetic candles and share a bowl of lettuce from that morning’s harvest. That small, deliberate sequence—technical sign‑offs followed by communal eating—turns a day of juggling systems into an evening that feels like home, and it closes the operational loop on the suit repair, greenhouse fix and dust‑power decisions made earlier.
narrationSegments.narrativeFunction: payoff / closing scene tying technical and social resilience
